aspects.says: A parameter is a new variable holding a copy of the argument's value, so assigning to it, primitive or reference, never changes the caller's variable, while a call through the copied reference changes the caller's object.
basis: section:Java Copies Every Argument, So Assigning to a Parameter Never Reaches the Caller's Variable

aspects.says: final on a parameter makes assigning to it a compile error but still lets the method change the object it refers to.
basis: section:Java Copies Every Argument, So Assigning to a Parameter Never Reaches the Caller's Variable

aspects.says: String, the wrappers and BigDecimal can't be changed, so subtract, ++ and += only give the parameter a new object, and a method that computes a new value must return it.
basis: section:An Immutable Argument Can't Be Changed, So a Method That Computes a New Value Returns It

aspects.says: An object that stores an argument shares the caller's object, so it copies it on the way in; an unmodifiable view is not a copy, and List.copyOf rejects null elements.
basis: section:A Method That Keeps Its Argument Keeps the Caller's Object

aspects.says: After a method assigns a new object to its parameter, every later change through that parameter goes to the new object, not to the caller's.
basis: section:Spot the Problem: a Default That Never Arrives

aspects.says: A method that changes its argument changes the caller's object, so a method that only reads its input works on its own copy.
basis: section:A Method That Changes Its Argument Makes That Change Part of Its Contract

aspects.says: A record's canonical constructor stores its components as given, and a final field doesn't stop the list it refers to from changing.
basis: section:A Method That Keeps Its Argument Keeps the Caller's Object

aspects.says: Every method of an unmodifiable list that could change it throws UnsupportedOperationException, even when the call would change nothing.
basis: section:A Method That Changes Its Argument Makes That Change Part of Its Contract
